name: Computer Vision Inspection
blurb: AI inspection of tablets, vials and packaging on the line.
title: Computer Vision Inspection
answer: AI vision systems inspect products on high speed lines and detect subtle defects older rule based systems miss, such as cracks, particles and print errors. Because they make or support release relevant decisions, they need the same validation as other inspection equipment, with a defined defect library and challenge sets.

reading.body:
AI vision inspection earns its place on a pharmaceutical line by catching defects that rule based systems miss, but that same role makes it regulated inspection equipment, not ordinary software.

The defects named here are cracks, particles and print errors on tablets, vials and packaging. These are release relevant findings, which is why the page pairs the capability with the obligation: a defined defect library and challenge sets, rerun after every model or camera change. The pattern is that the model is not the deliverable. The evidence that the model still works is.

For AI specifically, this is the point where a vision model stops being a quality project and becomes part of the batch record. A camera and model change is a change to an inspection method, so the challenge set is what keeps the validation claim true over time. The single 2024 study cited shows deep learning defect detection working in real time for pharmaceutical quality control, which establishes feasibility rather than adoption.

What the data does not cover is scale. There is no count of deployed lines, no defect escape rate, no false reject rate, and no cost figure. It also does not say which regulators or which specific validation standard applies, only that the same validation as other inspection equipment is needed. The compute and power side is absent entirely, so nothing here supports a claim about inference cost or on line hardware.

AI for Stability and Shelf Life Prediction

explainer:
Visual inspection checks products for defects: cracked or chipped tablets, foreign particles in vials, fill level, seal integrity, label and print errors. Manual inspection is tiring and inconsistent, and traditional automated systems use fixed rules that struggle with natural variation, producing false rejects that waste good product.

Deep learning vision systems learn what defects look like from labelled images and can distinguish real defects from harmless variation more reliably. Because inspection supports release decisions, validation is essential: a defect library covering all defect types, challenge sets of known good and bad units, predefined detection and false reject criteria, and requalification after any change to the model, cameras, lighting or product. Locked models and full traceability of decisions fit both current GMP and draft Annex 22.

developments.text: A study in Scientific Reports demonstrated deep learning based defect detection for pharmaceutical quality control in real time.
